rv.q: Zeldin’s script dives from black comedy to horror, while his staging gives us a brilliant compound of the ordinary and the eerie.

Menzies and D’Arcy, the entrancingly stubborn elder daughter, deliver a climax that sent a series of collective gasps of shock through the audience on the night I went – and which does full justice to the Antigone myth, on which Zeldin’s drama is based.
On its own terms, this is sucker-punch theatre, beautifully detailed and at times excruciatingly funny.

But all these quibbles can’t take away from the vivid family dynamic that Zeldin and his cast create here, which has affinities with his superb Inequalities Trilogy and 2023’s The Confessions, about his mother.
It is an accomplishment that this drama generates gasping shocks with such an ancient story.

The urn of ashes is constantly being decanted into a Ziploc bag in a tug-of-war that’s partly a farce, with Jerry Killick providing laughs as the sleazebag family friend. The shock revelation I can’t spoil.
It’s a muddled showing from Zeldin the writer.
The malnourished torpor appealed to the depressive maso­chist in me, but needn’t detain better-adjusted theatre-goers.
The Other Place is a ferocious whirlpool of a play that sucks you further and further down into a vortex that drowns you in man’s venality.
The Other Place does a simple thing in a sophisticated way.
It is strange, twisted yet terribly feasible, and utterly gripping.
Chris undergoes a three-part personality shift – reasonable patriarch to raging bully to a man weakened by his own misguided sexuality – that, in the space of a day, is not entirely believable.

Zeldin has the basis of a really interesting family drama and the tensions that emerge from the loss of a family member, but The Other Place feels slight and needs more time to establish the characters and make their desire to be free of their grief more tangible.
The 80 minutes fly by, and that goes to show how gripping this slick, modernised spin on Antigone is.
While there is nothing to fault in Zeldin’s writing, per se, it felt to me as if the play was unfinished.
But for all the skill and effort, and the insistence that it’s based on Sophocles’ Antigone, it doesn’t fly however hard they all pedal...

cn.t: Zeldin's modern Antigone adaptation divides critics, with standout performances from D'Arcy and Menzies widely praised. Some find it a searing, cathartic tragedy; others feel it's fatalistic and loses its way in murky psychodrama.
